title: New England's summer thunderstorms grow shorter and heavier, raising flash flood risk
summary: A growing share of New England's summer rain is falling in the form of heavy, heat-related showers and thunderstorms, raising the risk of flash flooding events across the region as the climate continues to warm. That's according to a new study by Brown University researchers published in Science Advances.

Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked peer-reviewed publication trusted source proofread The GIST Add to Preferred Sources Credit: Pixabay/CC0 Public Domain A growing share of New England's summer rain is falling in the form of heavy, heat-related showers and thunderstorms, raising the risk of flash flooding events across the region as the climate continues to warm. That's according to a new study by Brown University researchers published in Science Advances . The research drew upon 40 years of hourly weather station data recorded from 1980 to 2020 from 80 airports across New England. It showed that while the total amount of summer rain stayed largely stable over the study period, the nature of that rainfall changed significantly. Lighter, longer-duration rains decreased, while shorter, heavier downpours—which can quickly overwhelm wastewater drainage systems—increased substantially. Summer storms grow shorter and heavier The study is among only a few, the researchers say, that look specifically at New England's "convective precipitation"—the kind of rain that falls mainly on summer afternoons when high temperatures push moist air higher into the atmosphere, where that moisture quickly condenses and falls as heavy rain. "In research on convective precipitation, this area has basically been ignored because historically there are just fewer summer days where it's hot enough to get those vigorous thunderstorms," said Jared Kodero, the study's lead author and a Ph.D. student in Brown's Department of Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences. "But we found that since 2000 there's been a big increase in this convective activity, and those high-intensity rains are what cause a lot of problems in terms of flash flooding. "We attribute this to a poleward expansion of the convective belts that historically have been more prevalent in tropical regions and parts of the Midwest," Kodero added. In the second half of the study period, from 2000 to 2020, the average duration of summer thunderstorms decreased by nearly 40 minutes, even though total summer rainfall stayed the same. In other words, summer storms are growing more intense. The most intense storms—those that drop more than 10 millimeters (0.4 inches) of rain per hour—accounted for a 25% larger share of summer thunderstorm rainfall in the later part of the study period compared to the early part, the researchers found. Warming air and drier soils intensify downpours These shifting precipitation patterns are caused by several factors, the researchers say, all related to a warming planet. In general, a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, which can fuel heavier downpours. For every increase of one degree Celsius, air can hold about 7% more water. But that effect only explains half of the roughly 13% to 14% per-degree jump in extreme thunderstorm intensity found in the study. The rest is likely explained by a more unstable atmosphere and drier summer soils, which are related to the decrease in larger-scale, soaking precipitation. Large-scale rains are driven by collisions of warm and cold air masses. At the collision point, known as a front, warm air is pushed aloft, creating rain. Over the past century, polar regions have warmed much faster than midlatitude and tropical regions. That reduces the temperature differences of the air masses that tend to meet over New England, according to study co-author Jung-Eun Lee, an associate professor of Earth, environmental and planetary sciences. "New England is at that boundary where Arctic air and warmer air from the south often meet," Lee said.
